summary: Describes four extra FTP commands that BBN added to its servers so that users can create and remove directories, print the current directory, and move up to the parent directory. They were designed to work on systems with tree-like directories, such as Unix, Tops-20 and Multics.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a filing cabinet with folders inside folders. These commands let you make a folder, delete one, ask where you are, and step back out to the folder above.

questions: how do you create directories in ftp
subtitle: Directory commands for FTP on systems with hierarchical filesystems

tldr.problem: FTP servers on Unix, Tops-20 and Multics have tree-like directories, but the standard FTP protocol had no commands to create, remove or navigate them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four new FTP commands: XMKD to create a directory, XRMD to remove one, XPWD to print the current directory, and XCUP to change to the parent directory.
tldr.outcome: These experimental commands were adopted and simplified into the standard commands MKDIRCWD (make directory), RMD (remove directory), PWD (print working directory) and CDUP (change to parent) used in FTP today.

today: The four experimental commands defined in RFC 775 (XMKD, XRMD, XPWD, XCUP) were later standardized and are now commonly known as MKDIR, DELE (or RM), PWD, and CDUP. RFC 775 itself is not a standard; it documents the original experimental design that became the basis for modern FTP directory handling.

sections.title: FTP Commands for Directories
sections.content: This RFC defines four new commands to extend the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) on systems that organize files in tree-like directory structures. The commands were developed at BBN for its Unix servers but work equally on Tops-20 and Multics, and solve a key gap: the original FTP protocol had no standard way to create directories, remove them, or navigate between levels of the directory tree.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP could transfer files but could not create the folders they live in. These four commands fill that gap.

sections.title: The Four Commands
sections.content:
The RFC introduces four commands prefixed with X to mark them as experimental. XMKD (make directory) creates a subdirectory with a given name in the current working directory, or at a specified absolute path. XRMD (remove directory) deletes a subdirectory. XPWD (print working directory) returns the full pathname of the current working directory. XCUP (change to parent) moves up one level to the parent directory.

An important detail: when XMKD succeeds, the server responds with the absolute pathname of the newly created directory. This ensures clients can reliably refer to the directory, because on some systems like Tops-20 a relative directory name given to XMKD must be accessed by its full absolute path.
sections.plainLanguage: XMKD makes a folder, XRMD deletes one, XPWD tells you where you are, and XCUP takes you up one level. When you create a folder, FTP tells you its full address so you can find it later.

sections.title: Reply Codes
sections.content:
Each command has standardized response codes. XMKD returns code 257 on success with the directory name, 521 if the directory already exists, and codes for access denied, bad syntax or file system errors. XCUP uses the same success code (200) as the change-directory command it resembles, with codes for access denied, no parent directory, or system errors. XRMD uses codes similar to the file-delete command, with 224 on success. XPWD returns 257 with the pathname on success, or error codes for system problems or unimplemented commands.

The RFC emphasizes that reply code 257 is the only entirely new code introduced; others map to existing FTP codes or are taken from concurrent RFC 765.
sections.plainLanguage: Each command gets a number back: 257 means success for XMKD and XPWD, 200 for XCUP, and different numbers for errors like 'folder already exists' or 'you cannot do this'.
